raw_text:
Cardiac contractility modulation (CCM) is an implantable, bioelectronic therapy for patients with chronic heart failure who remain symptomatic despite guideline-directed medical therapy (GDMT). Contemporary heart failure guidelines emphasize four foundational drug classes for HFrEF and device therapy when indicated, especially implantable cardioverter-defibrillators and cardiac resynchronization therapy (CRT) for patients with electrical dyssynchrony [1,2]. CCM addresses a different unmet need: patients, typically in sinus rhythm with narrow or only mildly prolonged QRS complexes, who have persistent NYHA class III symptoms and left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) in the reduced or mildly reduced range but are not CRT candidates.

The therapy delivers relatively high-voltage, biphasic electrical signals to the right ventricular septum during the absolute refractory period. Because stimulation occurs after depolarization, it does not pace the ventricle or resynchronize activation; instead, it modulates myocardial biology and contractile performance. Early mechanistic studies showed acute augmentation of contractile state without increased myocardial oxygen consumption [3]. In canine heart failure models, chronic CCM improved LV function and attenuated remodeling [4]. Human biopsy studies suggested reverse molecular remodeling, including down-regulation of fetal and stress-response genes and up-regulation of calcium-handling genes such as SERCA2a and phospholamban [5]. Later experimental work extended these observations to microRNA-mediated SERCA2a regulation and metabolic remodeling through AMPK/PPAR-α signaling [6,7]. Mechanistic reviews now frame CCM as a myocardial “conditioning” therapy affecting excitation–contraction coupling, titin phosphorylation, calcium cycling, autonomic tone, and fibrosis rather than as an inotrope in the traditional pharmacologic sense [8].

Clinical development proceeded through small feasibility studies and randomized trials. The pivotal early double-blind crossover study enrolled symptomatic patients with LVEF <35% and showed improvements in quality-of-life and exercise-related endpoints, although placebo effects and crossover design complicated interpretation [9]. The FIX-HF-5 program then evaluated CCM in a broader systolic HF population; its rationale, device implantation approach, and baseline characteristics were described before trial completion [10]. The main FIX-HF-5 randomized trial met safety objectives but did not meet its primary efficacy endpoint in the full population [11]. However, prespecified and subsequent subgroup analyses suggested greater benefit among patients with LVEF ≥25%, normal QRS duration, and NYHA class III symptoms [12]. Echocardiographic studies further supported improvements in global and regional systolic function, mitral regurgitation, and reverse remodeling [13].

These signals led to a more focused confirmatory trial, FIX-HF-5C, enrolling patients with LVEF 25–45%, QRS <130 ms, and persistent NYHA class III/IV symptoms despite GDMT [14,15]. At 24 weeks, CCM improved peak oxygen uptake, 6-minute walk distance, NYHA class, and Minnesota Living with Heart Failure Questionnaire scores, with acceptable device-related safety [15]. The simplified two-lead Optimizer Smart system was subsequently evaluated in FIX-HF-5C2, showing comparable safety and performance while reducing hardware burden [16]. Longer-term observational data, including multicenter registries and single-center experiences, have reported sustained improvements in NYHA class, quality of life, LVEF, and reduced HF hospitalization compared with pre-implant periods [17,18]. Importantly, long-term electrocardiographic assessment did not show QRS widening, supporting electrical safety in follow-up [19].

Meta-analytic evidence is consistent with symptomatic benefit. An individual-patient-data meta-analysis across randomized CCM trials found improvements in peak VO₂, 6-minute walk distance, and health-related quality of life, with the most favorable signal in patients with LVEF 25–45% [20]. In patients with mildly reduced systolic function, pooled analyses of prior trial participants with LVEF 40–45% also suggested improvements in exercise capacity and quality of life, supporting the hypothesis that CCM may be especially useful at the interface of HFrEF and HFmrEF [21]. Eligibility analyses indicate, however, that only a minority of real-world HF patients meet trial-like criteria, making careful phenotyping essential [22].

Practical implementation resembles pacemaker implantation but requires attention to septal lead positioning, sensing, therapy delivery percentage, interaction with coexisting ICDs, and patient adherence to recharging [23]. Reviews emphasize that CCM should not substitute for GDMT optimization, revascularization when appropriate, valve intervention, CRT in eligible patients, or advanced HF therapies in end-stage disease [24–26]. Rather, it occupies a niche for persistently symptomatic ambulatory patients without CRT indications. Economic and systems considerations remain important, particularly because most evidence demonstrates improved function and quality of life rather than definitive mortality reduction [27,28].

The field is now expanding beyond classic HFrEF. Ongoing and recent studies are examining CCM in HFpEF and higher EF ranges, including AIM HIGHer, reflecting mechanistic interest in lusitropy, myocardial stiffness, and calcium reuptake [29]. Next-generation platforms may combine CCM with defibrillator capability or more sophisticated sensing algorithms [30]. Overall, CCM is best viewed as an adjunctive device therapy with credible mechanistic rationale and reproducible symptomatic benefit in selected patients, while definitive effects on hard outcomes and optimal positioning in modern GDMT-era care remain active research questions.
